chapter: Adventures with Galley Slaves (to p. 73), then Flight into the Mountains and Sancho's Errand

facts: The page opens mid-sentence: it would have gone hard on Don Quixote, but the convicts saw their chance and began trying to break the chain that tied them together
This distracted the guards, who could not decide between fighting Don Quixote and controlling the prisoners, and ended up doing nothing of use
Meanwhile Sancho gave Gines de Pasamonte a hand at removing his shackles, and Gines was the first in the gang to get free
Gines at once threw himself on the wounded guard and seized his sword and pistol
He threatened the other guards with them but held his fire, and they soon scurried away, partly from fear of the pistol and partly because of the stones the convicts were throwing
Sancho wanted to go at once to the nearby mountains, fearing the guards would raise a search after them
Don Quixote would not leave before talking to the convicts, who by now had stripped the wounded guard naked
He called them together and reminded them of what he had done for them and how much they owed him
He commanded them to go to Toboso and there lay the chain that had bound them together at the feet of Lady Dulcinea, and to tell how they were freed by his heroic feats
After that, he said, they could go where they pleased
Gines de Pasamonte spoke for all the convicts, saying they could not do any such thing now
A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with Don Quixote commanding the convicts to go to Toboso and tell Dulcinea how they were freed
Gines finished his refusal: instead of going to Toboso they must scatter and hide from the pursuit of justice
He proposed that they should each say prayers for their rescuer, since they could do that as they ran and hid
This put Don Quixote in a rage, and he demanded that Pasamonte go himself and carry the chain on his back
Pasamonte, seeing now the mental state of the man he was dealing with, motioned to the convicts to step back a few paces
From there the convicts began throwing a hurricane of stones at the knight and his squire
Sancho tried to hide behind his donkey, but Don Quixote and Rocinante were exposed to the full force of the storm of stones
In a short time both of them lay flat on the ground, very badly bruised
Pasamonte then ruthlessly attacked Don Quixote, beating him repeatedly with the brass barber's basin
He then banged the basin on the ground until it was almost smashed to pieces
Next the convicts stripped off Don Quixote's jacket and trousers
Sancho's cloak was taken as well
After hurriedly dividing the spoils they made off in different directions and were quickly out of sight
The chapter ends here
Chapter 6 opens, titled Flight into the Mountains and Sancho's Errand
As soon as Don Quixote and Sancho were able to take the road again they made for the mountains to hide for a time
They talked as they went about the ingratitude of some people
By night time they arrived at the gorges of the Sierra Morena
After searching a little they chose a resting place between two rocks in a grove of cork trees
But fate had it that the villain Pasamonte wandered in the same direction and arrived at the very spot where master and man were resting

glossary.cork trees: A type of oak tree native to the Mediterranean whose light, waterproof bark is stripped off about every ten years to make such things as bottle stoppers.

facts: Master and man, worn out with the sufferings of the day, had fallen into a deep sleep
Pasamonte recognized them, and seeing how soundly they slept, cast covetous eyes on the knight's horse and the squire's donkey
He judged the horse to be of little use and no cash value, but the donkey was sturdy

Taking it was no easy matter, because Sancho was anxious about the safety of his cherished Dapple in that wild country where robbers might prowl at night, and had arranged himself to sleep on the back of his beast
Crouched on his wooden saddle, Sancho slept as if he were in a feather bed
Pasamonte studied him in that state while he thought of his plan
After a while he cut four stakes of wood and quietly propped them under the four corners of the saddle
Then, gently loosening the saddle, he led the donkey out from under it and made off with the beast, leaving Sancho still mounted and undisturbed
At the break of day Sancho awoke, yawned and stretched, and instantly fell to the ground in a heap
He looked around in amazement to see what had happened and where Dapple was, but by that time she was many miles away
Sancho realized the trick that had been played on him and the loss he had suffered
He let go of his feelings so loudly that the rocks all around echoed with his wailing, and his uproar woke Don Quixote
A full-page engraving of a rider leading an animal away down a misty mountain track
The caption beneath repeats the line from page 75 about making off with the beast and leaving Sancho still mounted and undisturbed

Don Quixote tried to comfort his grieving squire
Sancho at last calmed down after Don Quixote promised him three of the donkeys he had at home
After eating what was left of their food for breakfast, the knight and squire resumed their aimless wanderings through the glens and ravines of the country
Presently they came upon what appeared to be signs that some unfortunate traveller had lost his way, and probably his life, in the wilderness
First they found a saddle cushion with a leather case strapped to it, both so rotten they must have been lying there abandoned for a long time
The case contained linen underwear, a pocket-book and more than a hundred gold coins
In the pocket-book were some sad love poems, which Don Quixote read with deep interest and sympathy
Sancho, with the permission of his master, stuffed the money in a pouch and thought he was richly rewarded for all he had gone through
Later on they came upon the carcass of a mule lying in a creek, still saddled, but half devoured by birds and beasts of prey
An old goatherd they met later was able to throw some light on the mystery
According to the goatherd the traveller was a lovesick shepherd who had wandered into those parts and gone stark mad
The shepherd was still haunting the mountains, running around almost naked and at times very dangerous to the people he met
A full-page engraving of the knight and his squire on a wooded mountain track, with a dead animal in the foreground
The caption beneath repeats the line from page 77 about coming upon the carcass of a mule
There is no story text on this page
The mad shepherd was dangerous to the solitary people he met
Don Quixote resolved to see him if he could, and during his stay in the mountains he did come across him twice, but to no purpose
In his more normal moments the madman would tell Don Quixote long tales of his romantic troubles, and then his fury would break out fresh, to the danger of those near him
It was perhaps the spectacle of this unhappy being and the loneliness of the surroundings that inspired Don Quixote with a new idea

He remembered that Amadis of Gaul had once, in a similar wilderness, decided to go mad and act out his desperate love for Angelica the Fair, who had rejected him, in order to prove the depth of his affection for her
Amadis had stripped naked and run about tearing up rocks and trees, and doing a thousand other things worthy of eternal fame
Don Quixote decided to imitate his example and told his intention to Sancho
Sancho asked what cause he had to go mad, since Lady Dulcinea had not disdained him or preferred someone else
Don Quixote answered that this was the point: there is nothing much in a knight-errant going mad for a good reason, and the thing is to do it for no reason whatever
He added that his long absence from Lady Dulcinea was cause enough
He said he would go mad until Sancho had taken a letter from him to her and returned with an answer
